title: Slavery in the Constitution
objective: After this level you can explain the three-fifths, slave trade and fugitive clauses, and how later Americans argued over what they meant.
summary: The Constitution never names slavery, yet three clauses protected it. Garrison called it a covenant with death; after 1851 Douglass argued it could be used to end slavery.

cards.headline: The words “slave” and “slavery” never appear in the original Constitution.
cards.body: Yet slavery shaped at least three of its clauses. Americans later fought bitterly over what that silence meant.

cards.headline: Counting three-fifths
cards.body: Level 32’s Great Compromise tied House seats to population, which raised a hard question: did enslaved people count? The Constitution counted three-fifths of the enslaved population when dividing House seats and direct taxes among the states. It called them “all other Persons.” The document counted them, but never named them.

cards.headline: Two more clauses
cards.body: Two other clauses dealt with slavery without naming it. One barred Congress from banning the importation of enslaved people before 1808. The other said a person “held to Service or Labour” who escaped to another state must be “delivered up on Claim.” Crossing a state line did not end the chase.

cards.headline: A covenant with death?
cards.body: Many abolitionists read these clauses as proof that the Constitution protected slavery. On July 4, 1854, at a rally in Framingham, Massachusetts, William Lloyd Garrison burned a copy and called it “a covenant with death, and an agreement with hell.”

cards.headline: Or a tool for freedom?
cards.body: Frederick Douglass once shared Garrison’s view. In 1851 he broke with him, arguing that the Constitution was a valid legal document that could be used for emancipation. Its words never named slavery, he argued, so they should be read in favor of liberty, not the framers’ hopes. Same document, opposite readings.

mascot.line: Notice the move: the clauses themselves are settled fact. The argument was over what they meant.

cards.headline: Slavery in the Constitution: explained
learned: The Constitution never uses the word slave or slavery
Three-fifths clause, 1808 slave trade clause, fugitive clause
Douglass after 1851: a tool for emancipation

questions.prompt: What did the Constitution say about the slave trade?

options.label: It banned the trade at once
options.rationale: It protected the trade for years.

options.label: Congress couldn’t ban imports of enslaved people before 1808
It never dealt with the trade
options.rationale: A clause did, without using the word.

options.label: Each enslaved person counted three-fifths toward it
options.rationale: That was the rule for House seats and taxes.

questions.explanation: Congress could not ban the importation of enslaved people before 1808.

questions.prompt: How did Frederick Douglass’s view of the Constitution change in 1851?

options.label: He decided it could be used for emancipation
He began calling it a covenant with death
options.rationale: That was Garrison’s phrase, which Douglass left behind.

options.label: He decided it named slavery openly
He joined Garrison in burning it
options.rationale: Garrison burned it in 1854; Douglass had broken with him.

questions.explanation: In 1851 Douglass broke with Garrison and argued the Constitution could be used to end slavery.

questions.prompt: The Great Compromise tied House seats to population. Why did that make counting enslaved people so important?

options.label: It decided which states could join the Senate
options.rationale: Every state got equal Senate seats.

options.label: It set the date for ending the slave trade
options.rationale: That was a separate clause, about 1808.

options.label: It changed how many House seats a state got
It decided who could vote for president
options.rationale: The clause was about House seats and direct taxes.

questions.explanation: Counting three-fifths of enslaved people added to a state’s population, and so to its House seats.
